title: Dana’s stories
source: Weren’t Born a Man (Hawksmoor, 2020), its draft I Rest My Case, and What Memories We Make (Hawksmoor, 2026)

themes.name: Highlights
themes.blurb: The best of Dana: Bowie, Superstar, the blues

stories.text: Singer, songwriter, actor and blues legend.
British Junior Water-Skiing Champion.
A teenage Dana meets a young David Bowie. He gives her her first guitar lessons.
“Dana is a very, very, very, very, very, very excellent songwriter.”
stories.by: David Bowie, BBC John Peel session, June 1971

stories.text: Bowie wrote “Andy Warhol” for Dana, and she sang on Ziggy Stardust.
Mary Magdalene in the original London Jesus Christ Superstar.
Over seventy albums, and twenty years of her own blues festival on Mustique.
TAM’s Mentor in Residence. She wrote The Best Christmas Ever for nights like these.
stories.alt: Dana, in black with red pockets, stands between David Shasha and Phill Brown at the Temple of Art and Music.

themes.name: Christmas
themes.blurb: Christmases past, from a pony under the tree to panto

stories.text: Dana’s mother’s clan was so close that thirty or more often sat down for Christmas lunch, with cousins popping up from all over the world.
Dana’s childhood Christmas tree was hung with marvellous lebkuchen from Schmidts, the German food shop she visited with her grandmother Oma.
One childhood Christmas, Nixi got a bicycle from her godfather, and little Dana got a pony called Rusty from her godmother, Jean Buxton.
Dana’s family opened Christmas presents by the tree around December 19th, then took off to the Alps to ski in Klosters.
While Dana played Mary Magdalene, a Christmas episode of Till Death Us Do Part was filmed in the Coach and Horses, the Superstar cast’s pub.
Offered a Mustique house over Christmas, Dana invited loads of friends. Lionel Bart came, and slept so much he left paler than he arrived!
For Christmas 1979 Dana played Principal Boy Dandini in ‘Cinderella’ in a freezing Eastbourne, belting ‘Don’t Rain on my Parade’ every night.
stories.said: “It was all utterly dreadful”

stories.text: After her chilly Eastbourne panto, Dana vowed never to do panto again, unless it’s with Julian Clary, whose camping it up would make it bearable.
In a freezing, rainy Eastbourne for panto, Dana’s only friend and consolation was her dog Sneezi, braving the arctic daily walks with her.
Dana loved sleigh rides with her father in Davos, under a huge fur rug, up to Certig for lunch, then back drowsy to the sound of the sleighbells.
stories.alt: Dana and her father in fur coats and wide black hats standing in falling snow among snowy fir trees.

stories.text: Dana sang over Christmas and New Year at Darjeeling’s Hotel Windemere, where the sun would burst through to reveal Kanchenchunga, Tiger Mountain.
Every year Dana and her mother joined the many Buxton relations at Kimberley Hall in Norfolk for a huge Boxing Day family lunch.

themes.name: Bowie fans
themes.blurb: Every Bowie story from her memoir and picture book

stories.text: In 1964 young David Jones wrote to John Bloom asking support for his band, The King Bees. It led to his first manager, and his first single.
After his set, lemon-haired Davie Jones of the Manish Boys took the brush from Dana’s hand and carried on brushing her waist-length hair.
stories.alt: Black and white portrait of a young Dana with long peroxide-blonde hair, wrapped in a fur coat, by Gered Mankowitz

stories.text: When Dana brought David downstairs, her father thought she’d had a girlfriend with her. David’s long lemon-yellow hair was misleading!
Young David Jones would pick Dana up from school and carry her ballet shoes home, or wait outside until her drama lesson was over.
David taught Dana ‘Love is Strange’ on guitar, and took her to a listening booth to hear his first single, ‘I Pity the Fool’.
David and Dana spent hours at the Gioconda café on Tin Pan Alley over one cup of tea. Neither dreamed of fame: they just wanted their songs published.
Even then, David dressed to be noticed. He and Dana went down to Carnaby Street, where he had outfits tailor-made, and heads turned when he walked by.
David’s first TV interview was for ‘The Society for the Protection of Long-haired Men’. In the clip, the twinkle in his eye says he’s having a laugh.
On Pinups, Bowie covered favourites from the years he and Dana spent hours in Soho coffee bars listening to the latest hits. His sleeve note said it:
stories.said: “These songs are among my favourites from the ’64-’67 period of London”

stories.text: David and Dana would head straight for the Green Room at ‘Ready Steady Go’ to network with the music business and the music press.
If a programme on mime artist Marcel Marceau came on, David would insist. He never watched brainless rubbish, he had a bright brain.
stories.said: “We must watch this”

stories.text: With Davy Jones of the Monkees on TV, David told Dana he would now be called David Bowie. But it was only ever a stage name.
stories.said: “He was David Jones all his life”

stories.text: Both on Decca, David and Dana shared a producer: the late Mike Vernon made David’s first album. The less said about ‘The Laughing Gnome’, the better!
On ‘Ready Steady Goes Live’, sixteen-year-old Dana sang ‘Love is Strange’, the song Bowie had taught her, with the Les Reed orchestra.
Dana and David moved in and out of each other’s lives for ten years. Even when he became an icon, she never saw him as ‘David Bowie, the star’.
stories.said: “He was my mate David Jones”
stories.alt: Polaroid of David Bowie in a hat, captioned David Bowie in Dana's hand

stories.text: David Bowie phoned Dana with a song he’d written half an hour before and came straight round to play it. It was ‘Space Oddity’, his first big hit.
stories.said: “I’ve just written this song half an hour ago”

stories.text: David brought Angie round to meet Dana and they instantly hit it off. Soon after, Angie renamed Dana’s flat ‘The Bunker’, and the name stuck.
stories.alt: Dana in a satin gown in her basement flat, The Bunker, full of rugs, books and a piano

stories.text: From 1969 David and Angie lived in Gothic Haddon Hall, Beckenham, for about £7 a month. The band slept on mattresses up on the minstrels’ gallery.
At Haddon Hall, if something like Japanese kabuki came on TV, Bowie would call everyone and they’d all climb onto his bed to watch.
stories.said: “Quick, it’s on!”

stories.text: Dana and David Bowie both auditioned for the stage show of ‘Hair’, on different days. Neither of them got chosen!
Bowie introduced Dana to manager Tony Defries. Soon David, Angie, Mick Ronson and Dana were like a family, with Defries as father figure.
stories.alt: Polaroid captioned Defries, Dana and Ronno at a dinner table, 1973

stories.text: Phoning Angie and Dana at midnight from America, Bowie raved about Roswell and aliens. His enthusiasm was so catching they both believed him!
stories.said: “You know it’s happened, it’s true, the aliens exist”
stories.alt: Dana and Angie Bowie, with spiky platinum hair, sitting close together

stories.text: Bowie wrote ‘Andy Warhol’ for Dana. She sang it on the John Peel Show in June 1971, and after hearing it with Ronno on guitar he recorded it himself.
stories.alt: Sleeve of Dana's Andy Warhol and Dizzy Heights single

stories.text: At Bowie’s 1971 John Peel session, Dana sang alongside him and the future Spiders from Mars. John Peel’s introduction said it all.
stories.said: “David Bowie and an astonishing number of friends”
stories.alt: A typed BBC contract form for the 1971 John Peel session

stories.text: In 1971 Bowie and Dana shared a demo album, his songs on one side, hers on the other. Only 500 were pressed. It’s now a priceless Bowie collectable.
stories.said: “I’m sure he regrets that now”

stories.text: “Dana is a very, very, very, very, very, very excellent songwriter.”
stories.by: David Bowie, BBC John Peel session, June 1971

stories.text: Dana walked to Glastonbury 1971 with Bowie. He finally played at 5am, and as he sang ‘Memory of a Free Festival’, the sun itself appeared.
At the end of a 1971 photo shoot with Dana, the photographer asked Bowie for a few shots. Beret off, hair back: one became the Hunky Dory cover.
stories.alt: David Bowie in a beret hugs Dana from behind in a studio photo session, 1971

stories.text: Dana suggested Dudley Moore play piano for Bowie, but Dudley didn’t turn up for the audition, so Rick Wakeman got the gig.
stories.said: “I wonder what ‘Life on Mars’ would have sounded like”

stories.text: Bowie meant to produce Dana’s album ‘Weren’t Born a Man’, but his career took off, so Mick Ronson produced it, with Rick Wakeman on piano.
stories.alt: Dana on stage in a red dress, singing into a handheld microphone under warm stage light.

stories.text: Dana wrote ‘Dizzy Heights’ about Bowie, the B-side of ‘Andy Warhol’, calling him “a carnival queen”, “a rock ‘n’ roll lady” and “ahead of his time”.
stories.said: “Not bad for a lyric written in 1972!”
stories.alt: Three international sleeves of the Andy Warhol and Dizzy Heights single

stories.text: Dana and Angie Bowie toured Britain’s radio stations promoting ‘Andy Warhol’. Someone put a beer in Dana’s hand, but she’s always loathed alcohol.
stories.said: “I definitely didn’t drink it”
stories.alt: Dana lounging on a bed holding a beer bottle, with Angie Bowie laughing beside her

stories.text: Dana’s album ‘Box of Surprises’ had a song about Bowie, ‘For David, The Next Day’. In 2013 he released an album called ‘The Next Day’. A message?
stories.said: “Who knows? Probably not”

stories.text: Dana told the whole Superstar cast David Bowie was in the audience. To her horror, David and Angie left at the interval!
stories.alt: Polaroid of David and Angie Bowie lounging

stories.text: In 1973 Dana and Angie flew to France on a Sunday to see Ronno at the Château d’Hérouville, where Bowie made Pinups. Back for Monday’s Superstar!
stories.alt: Black and white photo of Mick Ronson in a straw hat beside Dana at the Château d'Hérouville

stories.text: Dana was with Bowie the day before Hammersmith, 3rd July 1973, so she knew in advance he was going to kill off Ziggy Stardust.
stories.alt: Dana at a crowded party table with David Bowie, Jeff Beck and Mick Ronson at the Café Royal, 1973.

stories.text: Through the Pork crowd at Mainman, Andy Warhol’s Factory made the cover of Dana’s fourth LP, ‘Ain’t Gonna Play No Second Fiddle’.
stories.alt: Andy Warhol Factory screen print of Dana's face in pink, orange and black

stories.text: At the Sherry Netherland in New York, Bowie played guitar one night while Dana and Mick Jagger duetted on piano until dawn.
stories.alt: Dana in a red dress leaning on Bowie's grand piano

stories.text: In 1974 Dana photographed Mick Jagger visiting Bowie’s suite at the Sherry-Netherland. The picture went missing for her memoirs, but it’s back.
stories.alt: David Bowie and Mick Jagger reclining on a sofa, 1974, photographed by Dana

stories.text: David and Angie’s son Zowie was three when they all lived together in New York in 1974. He’s now film director Duncan Jones, his real name.
stories.alt: Polaroid captioned Zowie in New York of a small blond child in a green cardigan

stories.text: At Dana’s 1974 show at Reno Sweeney’s in New York, the crowd included Tom Waits, Bowie, Bette Midler and Raquel Welch. Dylan kept a low profile.
stories.alt: Tom Waits, David Bowie and Bette Midler at a crowded table at Reno Sweeney's, 1974

stories.text: As Bowie sang ‘Space Oddity’ from a capsule over the Diamond Dogs crowd, Angie clutched Dana’s hand. A wonderful, moving show.
stories.said: “Tell my wife I love her very much”
stories.alt: Michael Kamen and Angie Bowie on the Diamond Dogs stage at soundcheck in Montreal

stories.text: On the Diamond Dogs tour David wouldn’t fly, so he was driven through the night by limo. Sometimes Dana rode along to keep him company.
stories.alt: Polaroid of Geoff MacCormack, Angie and David Bowie backstage in New York

stories.text: On the Diamond Dogs tour Mainman took over the Beverly Wilshire. Defries had the Christian Dior suite, and Marc Bolan got the Marc Bohan suite!
stories.alt: Polaroid of Dana, Dean Stockwell in a cowboy hat and Angie Bowie in Hollywood

stories.text: Dana was with Tony Defries on Mustique when he made his final phone call to Bowie, telling him it just couldn’t go on anymore.
stories.alt: Tony Defries, bearded and smiling, with his arm around Dana

stories.text: In 1994 Dana and The London Blues Band played the Mick Ronson memorial concert at the Hammersmith Odeon, alongside Roger Daltrey and Roger Taylor.
stories.alt: Black and white photo of Mick Ronson in a straw hat beside Dana at the Château d'Hérouville

stories.text: Bowie built a Balinese house on Mustique but was hardly there. Its next owner found packing cases of Balinese statues Bowie never unpacked.
stories.alt: Wooden verandas of Bowie's Balinese-style house overlooking the sea on Mustique

stories.text: In 1994 Felix Dennis bought David Bowie’s Balinese-style house on Mustique and built a music room, where Dana’s band rehearsed with Mick Jagger.
stories.alt: Wooden verandas of Bowie's Balinese-style house overlooking the sea on Mustique

stories.text: Twenty days after a knee operation, Dana hobbled into the BBC on a stick to remember Bowie, who released a great new album three days before he died.
stories.said: “Good on you, David, it’s how you would have wanted to go”
stories.alt: Close-up of David Bowie's face, pale with orange hair, photographed by Dana

stories.text: Dana began 2020 singing in Rome at an event for Bowie’s birthday and anniversary, with dancers recreating Lindsay Kemp’s Ziggy-era moves.
stories.alt: Dana on stage at a Bowie tribute night in Rome, Lindsay Kemp on the screen behind

stories.text: In 1974 Dana filmed ‘Andy Warhol’ for Dutch TV show TopPop. In 2024 she recorded an updated version for Bowie’s 78th birthday in 2025.
stories.alt: Dana with dark curls and red lips in a gold corset against a red background, TopPop 1974

stories.text: Producer Tris Penna found the very first recording Dana made of ‘Andy Warhol’, with Bowie on guitar. It’s on the compilation What Memories We Make.
stories.alt: Moody black and white shot of Dana in a lit alcove, by Gered Mankowitz

stories.text: Dana named this photo book after a song on the record she made with Bowie in 1973. It’s a ‘coffee table book’, though she has no such table.
stories.said: “I don’t have such a table”
stories.alt: Dana, with long dark hair, sits at a table beside David Bowie, who rests his chin on his hand and gazes at her.

stories.text: Did Dana know Bowie and Elton were destined for megastardom? No. Bowie was a mate, Elton a guy she’d see at the Cromwellian.
stories.said: “Even when they became huge, to me they were still my old pals”
stories.alt: Polaroid by Dana of David Bowie in a cream double-breasted jacket against a green wall

stories.text: Pierre LaRoche created Bowie’s Aladdin Sane lightning bolt and did Mick Jagger’s make-up. He once ‘did’ Dana too, and made her look wonderful.
In 1973 Dana stayed with Bowie at the Château d’Hérouville near Paris, where Elton recorded several albums, including ‘Goodbye Yellow Brick Road’.
Mick Jagger showed Bowie the work of Guy Peellaert, booked for a Stones cover. David nicked the idea for his half-man, half-dog ‘Diamond Dogs’ cover.
Earl Slick played in Dana’s band in 1974, when he wasn’t on Bowie’s Diamond Dogs tour, and later on John Lennon’s ‘Double Fantasy’ album.

themes.name: Bob Dylan
themes.blurb: From the Savoy in 1965 to opening his 1997 tour

stories.text: At 16, Dana found her way into Bob Dylan’s press reception at the Savoy. Once the press had gone, he came over and they talked for 20 minutes.
stories.said: “There was definitely some sort of spark between us”

stories.text: No ticket for the CBS party at the Dorchester? Dana followed a canapé waiter through staff corridors and emerged via a hidden mirrored door.
Bouncers charged through the crowd to throw Dana out, but Bob Dylan stepped forward to kiss her hello and the bouncers retreated.
The day after the Dorchester party, Dana came home from school to hear Bob Dylan was on the phone. She dropped everything and went to his hotel.
Dana appears in ‘Don’t Look Back’, waiting in an empty Albert Hall. Manager Al Grossman reckoned she sang while surfing. It was water skiing.
stories.said: “Al Grossman says she sings while surfing”

stories.text: Dana gave Dylan her flowery bellbottoms, he wore them filming, and she was left with nothing much to wear, stuck in the hotel till he got back.
At a dull 1966 London press conference, someone mentioned Dana. The NME said Dylan brightened visibly and practically tore his face in half smiling.
stories.said: “Bring her out. I got some baskets for her”

stories.text: In 1966 Dylan told Dana he’d like her to record one of his songs, backed by Manfred Mann, who were having hits with his songs. It never happened.
stories.said: “Sadly, nothing ever came of this suggestion”

stories.text: Beatles and Stones played new tracks in Dylan’s suite; John Lennon passed out on the bed Dana was sleeping in. She was in it, he was on it.
Dana saw Dylan’s first ‘electric’ tour at the Royal Albert Hall in 1966. When the crowd booed, he just rocked louder. Afterwards they talked it over.
Dana’s minder John Bindon, not recognising the scruffy visitor, told Bob Dylan to get lost at her New York show. Poor Bindon later felt awful.
At Dana’s 1974 show at Reno Sweeney’s in New York, the crowd included Tom Waits, Bowie, Bette Midler and Raquel Welch. Dylan kept a low profile.
stories.alt: Tom Waits, David Bowie and Bette Midler at a crowded table at Reno Sweeney's, 1974

stories.text: For Dylan’s 50th birthday in 1991 a paper asked his friends for gift ideas. Dana’s: a ticket to India, to show him a good time so he’d smile more.
Dylan asked for Dana as opening act on his 1997 British tour. Two days before, he turned up at her door and they drank fennel tea.
Why ask for Dana in 1997, after all those years? Dylan had seen a good review of one of her Blues albums in Billboard, and it jogged his memory.
stories.said: “He said this reminded him how nice I was”

stories.text: Feet up on Dana’s sofa, Dylan told her how he nearly quit his 1987 tour with the Grateful Dead, till a singer in a little bar restored his confidence.
stories.said: “What a legend!”

stories.text: Before the tour Dylan told Dana he liked her songwriting, especially ‘Blue Temptation’, and at Wembley he listened to her whole set.
stories.said: “This was high praise indeed from His Bobness”

stories.text: Dylan browsed Dana’s bookshelves and took a book of quotations from world religions. It inspired her own book and CD, ‘Mirrors of Love’.
Seeing Sai Baba’s photo on Dana’s wall, Bob Dylan laughed. George Harrison had told him all about Him.
stories.said: “That’s the guy who materialises jewellery”

stories.text: Leaving Dana’s in 1997, Dylan said he was visiting George Harrison the next day. So Dana gave him some of her Sanskrit albums to pass on to George.
Needing a drummer at three days’ notice for Wembley with Dylan, Dana rang Queen’s Roger Taylor. He said yes and refused the paltry fee.
stories.said: “He was an absolute angel”

stories.text: After 70-plus albums, Dana’s First Love was mostly covers, including songs by two well-known men in her life: Bob Dylan and David Bowie.

themes.name: Jesus Christ Superstar
themes.blurb: The first London Mary Magdalene

stories.text: Dana wrote to the then little-known Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber: she should be their Mary Magdalene. They’d cast Yvonne Elliman the day before.
At the open audition for Superstar at the Palace Theatre, Dana wore skin-tight jeans and a T-shirt with a huge fist, and sang The Beatles’ ‘Get Back’.
Auditioning before Andrew Lloyd Webber, Tim Rice and Robert Stigwood, Dana was only trying for the chorus. Weeks later she opened as Mary Magdalene.
stories.said: “I always knew that I would be Mary Magdalene”

stories.text: Dana sang ‘I Don’t Know How To Love Him’ with tears in her eyes. The director told her friend Jean she’d be understudy, then turned to Dana.
stories.said: “You will be the new Mary”

stories.text: Hours later, Dana took the tube back to the Palace Theatre. The train was full of people reading evening papers with her name in the headlines.
With no costume to fit her, Dana played Mary in a long white caftan she had bought in Jerusalem years before. It had come from the Holy Land!
stories.said: “It was very appropriate when you think about it”

stories.text: Protesters, nuns among them, picketed Superstar as blasphemous, until the Archbishop of Canterbury saw it on opening night and gave it a thumbs up.
Dana and the late Richard Barnes often sang ‘Could we start again please’ looking at each other’s feet, so as not to burst out laughing.
King Herod was Paul Jabara, a hoot who brought the house down every night. He also wrote ‘It’s Raining Men’ for The Weather Girls.
Elaine Paige, later of Evita and Cats, began in Superstar’s chorus. So did Richard O’Brien, who walked out and wrote ‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show’.
Offered anything for her dressing room, Dana asked for a bed. While Jesus was betrayed and tried, Mary was offstage for ages, so she had a lie-down!
stories.said: “It’s not what it sounds like”

stories.text: When the famous Palace Theatre stage doorman Charles retired, the Evening Standard asked his best memory of all his years there.
stories.said: “Whenever Dana Gillespie came in”

stories.text: Superstar was Dana’s big breakthrough. Melody Maker called her the big surprise of the show, and The Times gave her the honours.
stories.said: “For musical pleasure, the honours go to Dana Gillespie’s Magdalene”

stories.text: While Dana played Mary Magdalene, a Christmas episode of Till Death Us Do Part was filmed in the Coach and Horses, the Superstar cast’s pub.

stories.alt: Polaroid of David and Angie Bowie lounging

stories.alt: Black and white photo of Mick Ronson in a straw hat beside Dana at the Château d'Hérouville

stories.text: Superstar’s drummer was 16-year-old Simon Phillips. When Dana left, so did he, to join her band. He went on to play with everyone from Asia to Zappa.
Her injured knee got so bad that Dana sang from the side of the stage. After 13 months as Mary she handed in her notice and went for an operation.
Later Dana recorded a duet with Tony Christie, ‘Magdalena’, written by Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber as a standalone single. Sadly, it got nowhere.

themes.name: One foot from stardom
themes.blurb: How close she was to today’s legends

stories.text: At the Marquee in Wardour Street, Dana tried never to miss the Yardbirds. Eric Clapton was her favourite: he played straight from the heart.
After his set, lemon-haired Davie Jones of the Manish Boys took the brush from Dana’s hand and carried on brushing her waist-length hair.
stories.alt: Black and white portrait of a young Dana with long peroxide-blonde hair, wrapped in a fur coat, by Gered Mankowitz

stories.text: At 15 Dana was offered a management and recording contract by Giorgio Gomelsky, manager of The Yardbirds. She never got round to signing it.
stories.said: “Sometimes, I wonder how my career would have developed”

stories.text: Eric Clapton was lined up as her guitar teacher, until ‘For Your Love’ hit the charts. He wrote to postpone, in perfect Italic handwriting.
Donovan played guitar on Dana’s first single, ‘Donna Donna’, in 1965. Weeks later ‘Catch the Wind’ was a hit, and Donovan was a star.
Dana supported The Hollies on Britannia Pier while they rode high in the charts, and her next single was a Hollies song, ‘Pay You Back With Interest’.
At 16 Dana cruised the Thames with the Rolling Stones for a stunt. Her job: look amazed, then drop her champagne glass. It made British Pathé News.
stories.alt: Black and white photo of teenage Dana with long fair hair, shading her eyes with her hand on a boat on the Thames.

stories.text: Paul Simon lived round the corner. Dana arrived to find him packing: ‘Sound of Silence’ had become a freak Number One in America.
The Cromwellian, three minutes’ walk from Dana’s home, hosted one of Jimi Hendrix’s first London shows. Rod Stewart and Ronnie Wood played there too.
