In 1971 Bowie and Dana shared a demo album, his songs on one side, hers on the other. Only 500 were pressed. It’s now a priceless Bowie collectable.
stories.said: “I’m sure he regrets that now”

stories.text: Dana suggested Dudley Moore play piano for Bowie, but Dudley didn’t turn up for the audition, so Rick Wakeman got the gig.
stories.said: “I wonder what ‘Life on Mars’ would have sounded like”

stories.text: At the end of a 1971 photo shoot with Dana, the photographer asked Bowie for a few shots. Beret off, hair back: one became the Hunky Dory cover.
stories.alt: David Bowie in a beret hugs Dana from behind in a studio photo session, 1971

stories.text: Elaine Paige, later of Evita and Cats, began in Superstar’s chorus. So did Richard O’Brien, who walked out and wrote ‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show’.
Superstar’s drummer was 16-year-old Simon Phillips. When Dana left, so did he, to join her band. He went on to play with everyone from Asia to Zappa.
Dana and her co-star Sarah Douglas both screen-tested for the villain Ursa in the second Superman film. Sarah won, but Dana’s test is on a DVD.
Did Dana know Bowie and Elton were destined for megastardom? No. Bowie was a mate, Elton a guy she’d see at the Cromwellian.
stories.said: “Even when they became huge, to me they were still my old pals”
stories.alt: Polaroid by Dana of David Bowie in a cream double-breasted jacket against a green wall

themes.name: Jimmy Page & Led Zeppelin
themes.blurb: The guitar god who played on and produced her first records

stories.text: In 1965 Dana sang ‘You’re a Heartbreak Man’, a single produced by Jimmy Page, on a Belgian TV special.
When Jimmy Page took over from Eric Clapton in Dana’s favourite band, The Yardbirds, he and Jeff Beck would sometimes come round to see her together.
John Paul Jones and Jimmy Page, later Led Zeppelin, played on Dana’s Decca sessions. Jimmy produced her single ‘You Just Gotta Know My Mind’.
Dana and Jimmy Page shared a love of Indian music, and would sometimes go together to see Ustad Vilayat Khan or Ravi Shankar in concert.
Black hair, dark eyes, always in black: Jimmy cut a striking figure. Dana remembers a nice, polite, gentle, lovely fellow, and a fabulous guitarist.
stories.said: “Jimmy was devastatingly good looking”

stories.text: Jimmy Page played guitar on most of the songs on Dana’s first album, ‘Foolish Seasons’, produced by Wayne Bickerton.
In France, Jimmy’s single ‘You Just Gotta Know My Mind’ came out as ‘You Really Haven’t Changed’. The label couldn’t even spell Donovan’s name!
Dana wrote to Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber saying she should play Mary Magdalene, and enclosed her Jimmy Page-produced single.
Jimmy Page and Robert Plant came to see Dana in her dressing room at Vienna’s English Theatre after her show.
Jimmy invited Dana to Led Zeppelin’s 2007 O2 reunion. She couldn’t collect the tickets, so Jimmy himself knocked on her door with them.
Over a million people applied for 20,000 seats. Dana sat in the VIP area near Jeff Beck and Lulu, with her guitarist Jake Zaitz over the moon.
Jimmy has come to see Dana and The London Blues Band at the 606 Club in Chelsea, and the band always buzz when they know he’s in the audience.
Dana spent her first ten years at Fishers Hill, a house built by Sir Edwin Lutyens. Jimmy Page loves Lutyens too: he has owned at least two.
Jimmy played on everybody’s records long before Led Zeppelin. To Dana he hasn’t changed at all, and more than 50 years on they are still friends.
stories.said: “Jimmy didn’t find fame suddenly”

themes.name: Elton John
themes.blurb: When Elton was still shy Reg Dwight

stories.text: At the Cromwellian, Dana’s local club, Long John Baldry’s band Bluesology had a young piano player called Reg Dwight, now better known as Elton John.
On cover-record sessions Dana met Reg Dwight: slightly chubby, with glasses and a schoolboy blazer with piping, and able to cover the big hits.
stories.said: “He was quite shy, but had a fabulous voice”

stories.text: Dana would bump into Reg at the Cromwellian and they’d say ‘See you at the studio’: Pye studios by Marble Arch, where the cover records were made.
On cheap ‘Top of the Pops’ cover LPs Dana sang beside Reg Dwight, who told them he’d changed his name to Elton John.
stories.said: “It was one of the best moves he ever made”

stories.text: Reg took his new name from Bluesology’s sax player Elton Dean and singer Long John Baldry. Could he have been a superstar as Reginald Dwight?
stories.said: “It was one of the best moves he ever made”

stories.text: In his autobiography ‘Me’, Elton recalls wailing through a Robin Gibb song while fellow session singers David Byron and Dana wept with laughter.
Covering ‘Back Home’, Elton John, David Byron and Dana had to sing as the entire 30-man England World Cup squad, and couldn’t stop giggling.
Elton kept singing on cheap cover albums even after his first big UK hit, ‘Your Song’. Always professional in the studio, he could be hilarious too.
Dana started collecting diamante sunglasses in 1970, even before Elton! She wore them on Mustique in her Blues Festival days.
On ‘Weren’t Born a Man’ Dana had Ray Cooper, Elton’s percussionist for nearly 50 years. Arranger Paul Buckmaster was too busy with Elton’s stuff.
In 1973 Dana stayed with Bowie at the Château d’Hérouville near Paris, where Elton recorded several albums, including ‘Goodbye Yellow Brick Road’.
Dana’s film ‘Mahler’ was soon overshadowed by Ken Russell’s next, ‘Tommy’, with Elton in his big boots and Ann-Margret in a sea of baked beans.
Did Dana know Bowie and Elton were destined for megastardom? No. Bowie was a mate, Elton a guy she’d see at the Cromwellian.
stories.said: “Even when they became huge, to me they were still my old pals”
stories.alt: Polaroid by Dana of David Bowie in a cream double-breasted jacket against a green wall

stories.text: Elton’s assistant Mike Hewitson played him one of Dana’s Sanskrit albums. His verdict? Dana can’t blame him: Sanskrit music isn’t to everyone’s taste.
stories.said: “Oh, I don’t like that at all”

stories.text: Elton once said his first band-pianist inspiration was Dave Rowberry. At a party Elton threw, Dana thanked him: Dave had spent years in her band.
Sir Elton John says spending time with Dana was very special: she was magical, and her laughter and kindness helped him overcome his shyness.
stories.said: “She knew my story before I did!”

themes.name: The Rolling Stones
themes.blurb: Mick, Keith, Ronnie and a Thames boat trip

stories.text: Yardbirds manager Giorgio Gomelsky looked after the Stones but never had them under contract. Andrew Loog Oldham stole them from under his nose.
Dana saw Brian Jones’s chaotic little house, where Keith and Mick were dossing too. Asked to see its recreation at a Stones exhibition, she said no.
stories.said: “I had seen the real thing, and had no need to see it again!”

stories.text: At 16 Dana cruised the Thames with the Rolling Stones for a stunt. Her job: look amazed, then drop her champagne glass. It made British Pathé News.
stories.alt: Black and white photo of teenage Dana with long fair hair, shading her eyes with her hand on a boat on the Thames.

stories.text: Ronnie Wood, then in The Artwoods, was a regular at Dana’s basement flat. His 1965 diary describes their get-togethers, often in the local Wimpy Bar.
After seeing Marianne Faithfull in Chekhov’s ‘Three Sisters’, Dana and Gered Mankowitz met her backstage, and Mick Jagger joined them for Chinese.
Dana signed as a songwriter to Immediate Records, the label of Stones manager Andrew Loog Oldham, and recorded demos of her new songs once a month.
On ‘Weren’t Born a Man’ Dana had Bobby Keyes on sax, best known for touring with the Rolling Stones and playing the sax solo on ‘Brown Sugar’.
Dana snapped Rolling Stone Mick Taylor on her Polaroid when he came round to The Bunker to collect his wife Rose, Dana’s friend.
Pierre LaRoche created Bowie’s Aladdin Sane lightning bolt and did Mick Jagger’s make-up. He once ‘did’ Dana too, and made her look wonderful.
At the Café Royal party for Ziggy’s 1973 ‘retirement’, the guests included the McCartneys. Dana sat with Mick Jagger, Lou Reed, Bowie and Ronno.
At the Sherry Netherland in New York, Bowie played guitar one night while Dana and Mick Jagger duetted on piano until dawn.
stories.alt: Dana in a red dress leaning on Bowie's grand piano

stories.text: In 1974 Dana photographed Mick Jagger visiting Bowie’s suite at the Sherry-Netherland. The picture went missing for her memoirs, but it’s back.
stories.alt: David Bowie and Mick Jagger reclining on a sofa, 1974, photographed by Dana

stories.text: Mick Jagger showed Bowie the work of Guy Peellaert, booked for a Stones cover. David nicked the idea for his half-man, half-dog ‘Diamond Dogs’ cover.
Mick Jagger bought land on Mustique early on. Bowie reckoned if it was good enough for Mick, it was good enough for him, and built a house there too.
Visiting Keith Richards in the late nineties, Dana heard how he climbed library steps for a Leonardo da Vinci book, went flying and broke two ribs.
In 2005 Mick Jagger sang ‘Dust My Broom’ and ‘Going Down’ at the Mustique Blues Festival with Dana’s London Blues Band. The bar was packed!
Mick Jagger called ‘Going Down’ an Albert King song. It was Freddie King’s, but Dana’s band didn’t tell him. They learned it in ten minutes.
Mick also sang ‘Honky Tonk Women’ at the 2005 Mustique Blues Festival, but Dana left it off the CD: not quite the right style for a Blues album!
At the Stones’ 2006 Twickenham show, as Keith Richards stepped forward for a solo, the lady sitting behind Dana leant forward proudly.
stories.said: “That’s my son up there”

stories.text: Ronnie Wood told Dana he left Necker Island because every day was planned for him. Mustique was far more relaxed.
stories.said: “You can’t tell a Rolling Stone to have breakfast at 9 o’clock!”

themes.name: The Beatles
themes.blurb: In Dylan’s hotel suite with the Fab Four

stories.text: In 1964 the press complained about the Beatles’ hair, but at the Marquee Dana spotted a singer whose lemon-yellow hair was far longer: Davie Jones.
At 16, Dana found herself in Bob Dylan’s hotel suite with the Beatles, then unquestionably the most famous group in the world.
stories.said: “That could only have happened in the Sixties”

stories.text: One night in Dylan’s suite, John Lennon put on a test pressing of a brand-new Beatles track, ‘Tomorrow Never Knows’, the final song on ‘Revolver’.
When the Beatles brought Cynthia, Jane Asher, Maureen and Patti Boyd to Dylan’s suite, Dana went back and forth making sure everyone got cups of tea.
Beatles and Stones played new tracks in Dylan’s suite; John Lennon passed out on the bed Dana was sleeping in. She was in it, he was on it.
Paul McCartney left early because he had to get Jane Asher home. Dana found him always really well behaved, and Ringo too.
The Beatles were at one of Dylan’s 1966 Albert Hall shows. When angry fans heckled his new electric sound, George Harrison called them ‘idiots’.
Decca boss Dick Rowe was famous as the man who turned down The Beatles, so it was only natural that he offered Dana a contract for two albums!
While the Beatles were hanging out with the Maharishi in the Sixties, Dana never got the chance to go to India. She finally went in the mid-seventies.
At the open audition for Superstar at the Palace Theatre, Dana wore skin-tight jeans and a T-shirt with a huge fist, and sang The Beatles’ ‘Get Back’.
At a party at Dave Clark’s flat over the Curzon cinema, everyone was there: Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr, Tony Curtis, Dusty Springfield, Nina Simone.
At the Café Royal party for Ziggy’s 1973 ‘retirement’, the guests included the McCartneys. Dana sat with Mick Jagger, Lou Reed, Bowie and Ronno.
Earl Slick played in Dana’s band in 1974, when he wasn’t on Bowie’s Diamond Dogs tour, and later on John Lennon’s ‘Double Fantasy’ album.
George Harrison’s Handmade Films produced ‘Scrubbers’. Whenever he came to watch, there was a buzz. Dana found him so polite and decent.
Seeing Sai Baba’s photo on Dana’s wall, Bob Dylan laughed. George Harrison had told him all about Him.
stories.said: “That’s the guy who materialises jewellery”

stories.text: Leaving Dana’s in 1997, Dylan said he was visiting George Harrison the next day. So Dana gave him some of her Sanskrit albums to pass on to George.

themes.name: Royals & Aristocrats
themes.blurb: Princess Margaret, maharajahs and a Baroness for a night

stories.text: Dana’s ancestors include Sir Thomas Fowell Buxton, who fought slavery with William Wilberforce, and Elizabeth Fry. Both appeared on the old £5 note.
Dana was born Richenda, said to be the name of a Romany gipsy princess, gifted to her kindly ancestors by a gipsy mother selling clothes pegs.
Tucked into the Fishers Hill nursery, little Dana asked her mother a big question: “What are we?” The answer still makes her smile.
stories.said: “We are Aristocrats”

stories.text: Dana’s father stitched the family crest on the piano stool himself: a stag’s head rising out of a crown, with the motto ‘Qui va piano va sano’.
While her parents watched Prince Philip play polo, Dana watched the Maharajah and Maharani of Jaipur. It sparked her lifelong pull to India.
Dana’s mother and father were photographed on their way to a garden party at Buckingham Palace, dressed elegantly as always.
A sister of the Jam Saheb of Jamnagar met Dana’s father at a London club about 50 years ago. She gave Dana her first book about Sai Baba.
Protesters, nuns among them, picketed Superstar as blasphemous, until the Archbishop of Canterbury saw it on opening night and gave it a thumbs up.
Colin Tennant, Lord Glenconner, bought Mustique in the fifties and gave Princess Margaret land there as a wedding present. For years he was its King.
Dana met Colin Tennant on the Cotton House steps in a striped pyjama suit. ‘You look ready for bed,’ she said. ‘And so do you!’ he laughed.
At the Cotton House, Princess Margaret would ask Dana to play ‘What Memories We Make’, from ‘Weren’t Born a Man’, calling it one of her favourites.
For Colin Tennant’s fiftieth on Macaroni beach the palm trees were painted gold. Princess Margaret, in silver, was the star of the show.
At a Macaroni Beach lunch with Dana’s house party, Princess Margaret set one guest straight on how to address her.
stories.said: “You must call me Ma’am, which rhymes with spam”

stories.text: At a Macaroni Beach lunch, Princess Margaret went for a dip in a floral swimming costume, keeping her head out of the water. She swam like a swan.
Told Istanbul’s Pera Palas Hotel was full, Dana rang straight back with a new name. They found her a double room right away.
On Mustique, Dana saw Princess Margaret mouthing the words to the saucy ‘King Size Papa’. Her secret? Her father, the King, used to sing it to her.
Dana knew Princess Margaret on Mustique for years, and gets very upset when she reads the negative things written about her.
stories.said: “She was always far nicer than she is ever portrayed in books”

stories.text: Every July Dana’s Buxton cousins threw a private three-day party at Kimberley Hall, dubbed ‘Toffstock’. Dana and her band played every Saturday night.
On Mustique Dana watched Prince William and Kate, now the Prince and Princess of Wales, dancing in Basil’s Bar. Once he lifted her right up!
When Basil asked Kate Middleton, now Princess of Wales, to dance, Dana’s guitarist Jake whispered a change of plan, and the band slowed right down.
stories.said: “He owes me one!”

themes.name: Animal Magic
themes.blurb: Ponies, cats, lion cubs and a goldfish called Mrs Perkins

stories.text: Dana’s father loved to tell how his grandmother ordered an elephant from India, then rode it around the Austrian countryside and into Vienna.
Her first newspaper appearance: winning a rosette at the local gymkhana, legs in a sideways splits on the saddle like a Thelwell cartoon.
After Sunday lunch, the family’s black cat Tonykins sat on Dana’s father’s stomach, slowly going up and down as he napped on the red velvet sofa.
One childhood Christmas, Nixi got a bicycle from her godfather, and little Dana got a pony called Rusty from her godmother, Jean Buxton.
Dad installed a marble fountain trickling onto Dana’s goldfish, Mrs. Perkins, just to watch dinner guests give in and dash for the loo.
Dana’s Norwich Terrier Sneezi was her best friend until she died aged 15. Boyfriends had to put up with her: love me, love my dog!
stories.said: “Sneezi and I were inseparable”

stories.text: With no live animals but her dog at home, animal lover Dana made do with cases of stuffed birds and animals. Within a year she’d added two real cats.
Visiting Israel over Christmas 1967, Dana dashed into the sparkling Red Sea at Eilat and came straight back out, face to face with an octopus.
stories.said: “I wasn’t expecting that!”

stories.text: Lost on horseback with Ashton, Gardner and Dyke, Dana headed for the nearest light. It was a funeral home, and they rode right in.
In a freezing, rainy Eastbourne for panto, Dana’s only friend and consolation was her dog Sneezi, braving the arctic daily walks with her.
Jorg’s Vienna flat was just like hers: oriental, full of art, smelling of incense. When his Siamese cats came out to greet him, Dana knew.
stories.said: “I knew I’d found a real home from home”

stories.text: Dana filmed the video with two lion cubs, Sheila and Georgie. One gave her a big kiss, and baby lion cubs, she says, smell delicious.
Singing in Eilat with the Joachim Palden Trio, Dana rode every morning on a horse reputedly once ridden by Sylvester Stallone. A perfect holiday!
At a wedding in Cairo Dana booked a gentle dawn camel ride round the pyramids. The owner only had an over-sprightly Arab pony that wanted to gallop.
At Sai Baba’s 75th birthday, His elephant Sai Gita joined the procession, with flags from all over the world, Vedic chanters and marching bands.
At the Udai Bilas Palace in Dungarpur, one of Dana’s favourite hotels, every room has a list of local birds for guests to tick off.
Ill for ten days in Russia, Dana was nursed by a rescued black kitten who lay purring on her neck. She named him Santosh, meaning happiness.
Dana loves the old Persian custom of passing round a basket of kittens to stroke between the courses of a long feast. She doubts it will catch on now!
David Shasha’s dachshund Lola, known as ‘the Hairy One’, kept Dana company while they wrote both her books, with a little help from biscuits.
These days Dana’s idea of bliss is a tapestry on her knee, a purring cat nearby and a bar of chocolate. She has made over one hundred cushions.
stories.said: “How Rock ‘n’ Roll is that!”

themes.name: Movies
themes.blurb: Hammer horror, Ken Russell, Holmes and Watson

stories.text: Italians at the Cromwellian wanted groovy extras. Dana turned up with her guitar, white boots and mini skirt, and landed in ‘Fumo di Londra’.
stories.said: “Alberto was the biggest name in Italian film at the time”

stories.text: At sixteen Dana wrote a song for ‘The Secrets of the Windmill Girls’ and foolishly sold it outright for £25, then sang it in the film.
Dana appears in ‘Don’t Look Back’, waiting in an empty Albert Hall. Manager Al Grossman reckoned she sang while surfing. It was water skiing.
stories.said: “Al Grossman says she sings while surfing”

stories.text: In 1966 Dana was an extra in John Frankenheimer’s motor-racing movie ‘Grand Prix’, starring James Garner, Yves Montand and Eva Marie Saint.
Hammer Films, a British institution for horror and cave girl fantasies, gave Dana a non-speaking dance-floor part in ‘The Vengeance of She’.
To win a Hammer Films part, Dana fasted 21 days on water and lemon juice. She got the role, then rediscovered the crew’s food trolley.
Hammer cast Dana in ‘The Lost Continent’ because a waterski champion could spend a lot of time walking on the ‘sea’. It was three inches deep.
Bacon sandwiches all day! Dana looks thinner in some shots of ‘The Lost Continent’ and larger in others. Luckily her chamois costume stretched.
stories.said: “It wasn’t my fault; I blame the food trolley”

stories.text: In ‘The Lost Continent’ Dana wore two huge balloons on her shoulders. Watching incognito in Fulham, she heard the audience fall about laughing.
stories.said: “Thank goodness no one recognised me on their way out”

stories.text: In ‘Hold on: It’s the Dave Clark Five’ Dana shared the cast list with Lulu, Richard Chamberlain, Charles de Gaulle and Nikita Khrushchev!
stories.said: “Check it out if you don’t believe me!”

stories.text: At 20 Dana was a guest on BBC antiques quiz ‘Going for a Song’. That week it was all about silver, and she lost to DJ Mike Raven.
stories.said: “I don’t know my hallmarks”

stories.text: While Dana played Mary Magdalene, a Christmas episode of Till Death Us Do Part was filmed in the Coach and Horses, the Superstar cast’s pub.
Reading Juno for Sir Peter Hall’s ‘The Tempest’, Dana was awful. Asked to sing the words instead, she invented a melody on the spot.
stories.said: “Right, the part is yours”

stories.text: Every night of ‘The Tempest’ Dana swayed high above Sir John Gielgud on a throne built like a huge peacock. And she hates heights!
Ken Russell cast Dana as opera singer Anna von Mildenburg in ‘Mahler’ without an audition. She just went to his house for a chat.
Ken Russell gave Dana 24 hours to find a simpler tune for a scene in ‘Mahler’. She wrote ‘Alma’s Song’ that night. It still earns her royalties.
Filming meant hours of waiting, so on the ‘Mahler’ set Dana took up embroidering tapestries. Not very rock ‘n’ roll, but it passed the time.
On La Palma Dana played Ajor in Hammer’s ‘The People That Time Forgot’, fighting prehistoric beasts with men hidden inside them.
Dana and her co-star Sarah Douglas both screen-tested for the villain Ursa in the second Superman film. Sarah won, but Dana’s test is on a DVD.
Dana appeared three times on BBC’s ‘Seaside Special’, once as compere. A paper called her the female equivalent of Bruce Forsyth.
stories.said: “I don’t remember having to do a twirl!”

stories.text: ‘The Hound of the Baskervilles’ had Peter Cook as Holmes, Dudley Moore as Watson, plus Terry-Thomas, Kenneth Williams and Spike Milligan.
stories.said: “What could possibly go wrong?”

stories.text: For a swamp scene with Hugh Griffith, Dana stood neck-deep in heated water in a studio hole all day. They went redder and redder.
Dudley Moore had the cast in fits on ‘The Hound of the Baskervilles’, so the make-up girl had to work overtime patching up their faces.
Dana acted in Nicholas Roeg’s ‘Bad Timing’ with Art Garfunkel and Harvey Keitel, and recorded Blues for it. Filming took her to Vienna.
In Mai Zetterling’s ‘Scrubbers’ Dana played kindly warden Budd, alongside Kathy Burke, Miriam Margolyes and Robbie Coltrane.
George Harrison’s Handmade Films produced ‘Scrubbers’. Whenever he came to watch, there was a buzz. Dana found him so polite and decent.
In the crime movie ‘Bones’ Dana played Monika, alongside Bryan Brown, Cheri Lunghi, Tom Wilkinson and fellow Hammer star Ingrid Pitt.
Dana played Mahler’s Anna von Mildenburg twice: for Ken Russell, and in an Austrian version, ‘To Live, I will Die’.
David Hare’s ‘Strapless’, with Bruno Ganz, Bridget Fonda and Hugh Laurie, premiered at Cannes. Dana can’t remember a thing about her role!
In ITV’s ‘Byron’s Mine’ Dana played a psychic medium opposite Leslie Phillips, and several of her Blues songs made the soundtrack.

themes.name: Move Your Body Close To Me
themes.blurb: The story of her Austrian hit

stories.text: An old man’s scratchy cassette in Dubai gave Dana a melody. It became ‘Move Your Body Close To Me’, which won the Golden Carinthia and hit the charts.
Dana sang lead on the Mojo Blues Band’s 1982 LP ‘Rockin’ Pneumonia and the Boogie Woogie Flu’. It sold well, and led to TV shows in three countries.
Dana persuaded Austrian label Bellaphon she had a hit. Recorded when synthesisers ruled, ‘Move Your Body Close To Me’ had a hypnotic, oriental feel.
Released in Austria, Germany and Switzerland, the single sat in the shops for 11 months. Nobody was buying it, but Dana still believed in it.
Everyone said Dana was mad to enter an oriental song in a pop festival for the Golden Carinthia, a gold statue of a singer holding a microphone.
Dana in silver sequins and her long-haired band, the Cobras, looked and sounded like nobody else. They won the Golden Carinthia.
stories.said: “We were completely different to everyone else”

stories.text: Once the win was on TV, the song was played everywhere. Austrian papers called her ‘Dana Move Your Body Close To Me Gillespie’ for years.
The song became a big hit in Austria, in a top 10 with Roy Orbison, U2, Marc Almond and Kylie and Jason, and charted in Switzerland and Germany.
Dana told English record companies how well the song was selling in Europe, but none would release it in Britain.
Dana filmed the video with two lion cubs, Sheila and Georgie. One gave her a big kiss, and baby lion cubs, she says, smell delicious.
The cover of the ‘Move Your Body Close To Me’ single was drawn by the father of Erik Trauner, founder of the Mojo Blues Band.

stories.kicker: On the road with the Cobras
stories.text: The hit filled Dana’s diary, so she and the Cobras hit the road. The single went on the album ‘Solid Romance’, with its oriental, Arabic feel.
Next LP ‘It Belongs To Me’ kept the oriental sound but didn’t do as well. Mind you, Bowie took three years to follow up ‘Space Oddity’!
In 1983 Dana filmed videos for ‘It Belongs To Me’ and ‘In Danger Tonight’ at Marrakesh’s Palais Badi. In local costume she felt at home.
stories.said: “Morocco is still one of my favourite countries on this planet”

stories.text: In Vienna Dana signed to Gig Records, whose boss Markus Spiegel had a smash with Falco’s ‘Rock Me Amadeus’. She made three LPs for him.
After the hit, Erik Trauner said Dana wasn’t being true to the Blues. It was just what she needed to hear, and she headed home to London.
Dana re-recorded her hit, working with keyboard player Tim Cross, for her 2001 album ‘In the Garden of Heavenly Peace’.
Vienna made Dana strong again, and gave her good musicians and a great club in Jazzland. And it gave her a hit.
stories.said: “The city gave me a hit with ‘Move Your Body Close To Me’”

themes.name: Vienna
themes.blurb: Her second home, Jazzland and the Mojo Blues Band

stories.text: Dana’s father loved to tell how his grandmother ordered an elephant from India, then rode it around the Austrian countryside and into Vienna.
Dana acted in Nicholas Roeg’s ‘Bad Timing’ with Art Garfunkel and Harvey Keitel, and recorded Blues for it. Filming took her to Vienna.
Mai Zetterling cast Dana in ‘Playthings’ at Vienna’s English Theatre in 1980. Every character was an object: Dana was a Ceiling and a Floor.
Jimmy Page and Robert Plant came to see Dana in her dressing room at Vienna’s English Theatre after her show.
Hearing bottleneck Blues across a crowded Vienna café, Dana sang her way through the crowd to the guitarist: Erik Trauner of the Mojo Blues Band.
After a few songs in the cellars of Jazzland, the late owner Axel Melhardt offered Dana a gig on the spot. Decades later she still goes back to sing.
In Vienna in 1980 Dana met Al Cook, who only plays Blues from the twenties and thirties. Years later they recorded an album in his cellar studio.
For three years Dana stayed at Erik Trauner’s rooftop flat. They bought Blues LPs, talked Blues, learned Blues songs and went to Blues gigs.
Dana told Erik Trauner musicians must always look smarter than their audience. Slowly the scruffy Mojo Blues Band smartened up.
Dana sang lead on the Mojo Blues Band’s 1982 LP ‘Rockin’ Pneumonia and the Boogie Woogie Flu’. It sold well, and led to TV shows in three countries.
In 1983 Dana and the Mojo Blues Band supported Chuck Berry in Austria and Belgium. He never rehearsed: every musician knew his songs.
An old man’s scratchy cassette in Dubai gave Dana a melody. It became ‘Move Your Body Close To Me’, which won the Golden Carinthia and hit the charts.
Dana in silver sequins and her long-haired band, the Cobras, looked and sounded like nobody else. They won the Golden Carinthia.
stories.said: “We were completely different to everyone else”

stories.text: Seeking a painter for an LP cover, Dana met artist Jorg Huber at the Metropole. At 2am she followed his footprints through the snow to his studio.
Jorg’s Vienna flat was just like hers: oriental, full of art, smelling of incense. When his Siamese cats came out to greet him, Dana knew.
stories.said: “I knew I’d found a real home from home”

stories.text: In Vienna Dana signed to Gig Records, whose boss Markus Spiegel had a smash with Falco’s ‘Rock Me Amadeus’. She made three LPs for him.
Dana played Mahler’s Anna von Mildenburg twice: for Ken Russell, and in an Austrian version, ‘To Live, I will Die’.
Dana and Viennese boogie-woogie pianist Joachim Palden recorded their first live album at Jazzland, December 7th to 9th 1990.
A misprint turned Dana’s song ‘Fine and Fancy Free’ into ‘Fine and Fanny Free’. Then the promo for her ‘Big Boy’ album called it ‘Bog Boy’!
Dana sold her beloved Citroën DS, ‘the Goddess’, to boogie-woogie pianist Joachim Palden. She visits it in Vienna, and wrote ‘Crazy ’Bout My DS’.
Through most of the Nineties Dana hosted ‘Globetrotting with Gillespie’ on Vienna’s Blue Danube Radio: Indian, African, Arabic and Blues music.
In 1995 Vienna’s Wolf Records asked Dana for an album. It grew to three, and every song title had the word ‘Blue’ in it.
stories.said: “I guess one can say I was going through my Blue Period!”

stories.text: Vienna made Dana strong again, and gave her good musicians and a great club in Jazzland. And it gave her a hit.
stories.said: “The city gave me a hit with ‘Move Your Body Close To Me’”

stories.text: Vienna is second only to London in Dana’s heart. She first went there broken and unhappy, and felt the city nurture her and make her strong.
stories.said: “Vienna is the place that has given me the most pleasure”

themes.name: India
themes.blurb: Rajasthan, Bombay, bhajans and the India Blues tour

stories.text: While her parents watched Prince Philip play polo, Dana watched the Maharajah and Maharani of Jaipur. It sparked her lifelong pull to India.
Dana’s father loved to tell how his grandmother ordered an elephant from India, then rode it around the Austrian countryside and into Vienna.
In the mid-seventies Dana finally got to India, touring Rajasthan’s triangle of Jaipur, Jodhpur and Udaipur. She fell in love with the country.
A sister of the Jam Saheb of Jamnagar met Dana’s father at a London club about 50 years ago. She gave Dana her first book about Sai Baba.
In the mid-eighties, with nothing to read on a night train from Davos, Dana borrowed ‘Man of Miracles’. By Vienna she knew she must go to India.
stories.said: “How little I knew”

stories.text: Soon after that night train, Dana flew to Bombay, then Bangalore, then rode a taxi five hours over bad roads to the village of Puttaparthi.
Dana learned bhajans in Sanskrit and Hindi from cheap Indian cassettes that fell apart, then recorded her own under the name ‘Third Man’.
At a Rippon Club concert Dana’s band had Ehsaan on guitar and Loy on keyboards, now of famous Indian trio Shankar-Ehsaan-Loy.
Singing for the Taj Hotel Group with Joachim Palden paid little, but they stayed in five-star hotels and lived like kings, or Maharajahs.
For Sai Baba’s 70th birthday He asked for Dana’s Western music, so she sang the Blues to a stadium crowd, with songs like ‘I Sigh For You’.
At Bombay’s Taj Mahal Palace with the cricket teams, Dana’s calls kept going to Australian cricketer Jason Gillespie, and his to her!
The hotel operator nearly fainted at the name. Indian superstar Jagjit Singh collected Dana from the Taj and let her write English words to his songs.
Dana sang a mantra with violinist Chandru’s Bollywood Strings Orchestra in London, then brought him to India for Baba’s 75th birthday.
Dana’s 2002 British Council tour of India covered eleven cities and twenty-two concerts, and not one bag was lost or one plane late.
The 2002 Blues tour ran from Goa to Cochin, Bombay to Delhi and Calcutta, with Qawali music at Delhi’s Sufi shrine of Nizamuddin.
Dana sang over Christmas and New Year at Darjeeling’s Hotel Windemere, where the sun would burst through to reveal Kanchenchunga, Tiger Mountain.
In Darjeeling at Christmas, Dana sang ‘It Ain’t Necessarily So’ to a room of nuns, then remembered the chorus line about the Bible.
As Sai Baba served the savoury food, Dana silently wished for dessert. Without turning round, He stirred a bowl of paysam and handed it to her.

stories.kicker: A rainbow sari in the rain
stories.text: At Baba’s 80th birthday it drizzled, so Dana sang outside the tent, soaked. Her rainbow and gold sari, a gift from Baba, hid the rain.
At the Udai Bilas Palace in Dungarpur, one of Dana’s favourite hotels, every room has a list of local birds for guests to tick off.
In Puttaparthi Dana rang U. Srinivas, India’s most famous mandolin player, out of the blue. He said it would be an honour to play on her tracks.
Mumbai’s Taj Mahal Palace is one of Dana’s favourite places on earth. In 2014 she sang its praises in BBC documentary ‘Hotel India’.
stories.said: “And as for the city, it really rocks”

stories.text: Dana filmed an episode of ‘Around My World in Sixty Songs’ on Marine Drive in Mumbai, the city she still calls Bombay.
stories.alt: Dana, smiling in a red shirt, by the sea on Marine Drive in Mumbai with the city skyline behind her.

stories.text: A dosa: batter cooked very thin on a hot plate, then dipped into chutneys. It’s Dana’s perfect breakfast in Mumbai, or Bombay as she knows it.
stories.said: “This is my idea of a perfect breakfast in Mumbai”

stories.text: Sitting at Fatehpur Sikri, Dana feels what she always feels in India.
stories.said: “I always feel in my heart that I am coming home!”

themes.name: Mustique
themes.blurb: Island life, Princess Margaret and the blues festival

stories.text: At the Cotton House, Princess Margaret would ask Dana to play ‘What Memories We Make’, from ‘Weren’t Born a Man’, calling it one of her favourites.
Offered a Mustique house over Christmas, Dana invited loads of friends. Lionel Bart came, and slept so much he left paler than he arrived!
At a Macaroni Beach lunch, Princess Margaret went for a dip in a floral swimming costume, keeping her head out of the water. She swam like a swan.
Needing a drummer at three days’ notice for Wembley with Dylan, Dana rang Queen’s Roger Taylor. He said yes and refused the paltry fee.
stories.said: “He was an absolute angel”

stories.text: Dana met Colin Tennant on the Cotton House steps in a striped pyjama suit. ‘You look ready for bed,’ she said. ‘And so do you!’ he laughed.
In the early 1970s Mustique had six or seven houses and dirt-track roads, and evenings at the Cotton House were often by candlelight.
For Colin Tennant’s fiftieth on Macaroni beach the palm trees were painted gold. Princess Margaret, in silver, was the star of the show.
Basil Charles stepped onto Mustique just as Colin Tennant needed a barman for a lunch with Princess Margaret. It changed his life forever.
Dana’s old friend Basil Charles began selling drinks at the harbour. Basil’s Bar became world-famous, and the Queen awarded him the OBE in 2005.
Colin Tennant, Lord Glenconner, bought Mustique in the fifties and gave Princess Margaret land there as a wedding present. For years he was its King.
Dana was with Tony Defries on Mustique when he made his final phone call to Bowie, telling him it just couldn’t go on anymore.
stories.alt: Tony Defries, bearded and smiling, with his arm around Dana

stories.text: At a Macaroni Beach lunch with Dana’s house party, Princess Margaret set one guest straight on how to address her.
stories.said: “You must call me Ma’am, which rhymes with spam”

stories.text: For 20 years Dana and Basil Charles ran the Mustique Blues Festival. Her festival CDs raised money for children on neighbouring St. Vincent.
stories.alt: Dana in a bright pink outfit singing on an outdoor stage beside guitarist Ian Siegal in a white suit and bandana.

stories.text: Nigel Kennedy joined the London Blues Band at the Mustique Blues Festival: not his usual style! Ronnie Wood, a friend since the sixties, played too.
Peter Golding, famous in Chelsea for stretch jeans when no one else had them, sang and played harmonica in Mustique. Dana still has two pairs.
Big Jay McNeely turned professional on sax in 1949, the year Dana was born. They made a duets album, Cherry Pie, and his honking sax wowed Mustique.
stories.alt: Dana and saxophonist Big Jay McNeely singing together into microphones on stage, a bass guitarist behind them.

stories.text: Pictured on Mustique in her Blues Festival days, Dana has collected diamante sunglasses since 1970.
On Mustique, Dana saw Princess Margaret mouthing the words to the saucy ‘King Size Papa’. Her secret? Her father, the King, used to sing it to her.
Mick Jagger bought land on Mustique early on. Bowie reckoned if it was good enough for Mick, it was good enough for him, and built a house there too.
Dana knew Princess Margaret on Mustique for years, and gets very upset when she reads the negative things written about her.
stories.said: “She was always far nicer than she is ever portrayed in books”

stories.text: Bowie built a Balinese house on Mustique but was hardly there. Its next owner found packing cases of Balinese statues Bowie never unpacked.
stories.alt: Wooden verandas of Bowie's Balinese-style house overlooking the sea on Mustique

stories.text: Mick Jagger called ‘Going Down’ an Albert King song. It was Freddie King’s, but Dana’s band didn’t tell him. They learned it in ten minutes.
Ronnie Wood told Dana he left Necker Island because every day was planned for him. Mustique was far more relaxed.
stories.said: “You can’t tell a Rolling Stone to have breakfast at 9 o’clock!”

stories.text: Mick also sang ‘Honky Tonk Women’ at the 2005 Mustique Blues Festival, but Dana left it off the CD: not quite the right style for a Blues album!
Dana ran the Mustique Blues Festival with Basil for 20 years, and went back in 2020 for its 25th anniversary with keyboard star Dino Baptiste.
When Basil asked Kate Middleton, now Princess of Wales, to dance, Dana’s guitarist Jake whispered a change of plan, and the band slowed right down.
stories.said: “He owes me one!”

stories.text: On Mustique Dana watched Prince William and Kate, now the Prince and Princess of Wales, dancing in Basil’s Bar. Once he lifted her right up!
After closing time at Basil’s Bar, Dana sang the Blues unaccompanied while Basil swung along. Together they dreamed up the Mustique Blues Festival.
Basil flew to New York for a white upright piano. The next January, the first Mustique Blues Festival began, raising money for St. Vincent’s children.
In 2005 Mick Jagger sang ‘Dust My Broom’ and ‘Going Down’ at the Mustique Blues Festival with Dana’s London Blues Band. The bar was packed!
In 1994 Felix Dennis bought David Bowie’s Balinese-style house on Mustique and built a music room, where Dana’s band rehearsed with Mick Jagger.
stories.alt: Wooden verandas of Bowie's Balinese-style house overlooking the sea on Mustique

themes.name: Childhood
themes.blurb: Growing up, from Woking to the Marquee

stories.text: Dana’s ancestors include Sir Thomas Fowell Buxton, who fought slavery with William Wilberforce, and Elizabeth Fry. Both appeared on the old £5 note.
Dana’s mother’s clan was so close that thirty or more often sat down for Christmas lunch, with cousins popping up from all over the world.
Dana’s childhood Christmas tree was hung with marvellous lebkuchen from Schmidts, the German food shop she visited with her grandmother Oma.
One childhood Christmas, Nixi got a bicycle from her godfather, and little Dana got a pony called Rusty from her godmother, Jean Buxton.
Dana’s father loved to tell how his grandmother ordered an elephant from India, then rode it around the Austrian countryside and into Vienna.
Dana spent her first ten years at Fishers Hill, a house built by Sir Edwin Lutyens. Jimmy Page loves Lutyens too: he has owned at least two.
After Sunday lunch, the family’s black cat Tonykins sat on Dana’s father’s stomach, slowly going up and down as he napped on the red velvet sofa.
Dana’s father stitched the family crest on the piano stool himself: a stag’s head rising out of a crown, with the motto ‘Qui va piano va sano’.
Dana was born Richenda, said to be the name of a Romany gipsy princess, gifted to her kindly ancestors by a gipsy mother selling clothes pegs.
Dana’s family opened Christmas presents by the tree around December 19th, then took off to the Alps to ski in Klosters.
Dana’s Norwich Terrier Sneezi was her best friend until she died aged 15. Boyfriends had to put up with her: love me, love my dog!
stories.said: “Sneezi and I were inseparable”

stories.text: Born Richenda Antoinette de Winterstein Gillespie on March 30th, 1949, at 12.15am in Woking Hospital, Surrey.
A milkman spotted her in cowboy boots and a Davy Crockett hat. At ten she told her mother everyone must call her Dana: she was going to be famous.
stories.said: “Here’s Dangerous Dana from Alabama”

stories.text: Tucked into the Fishers Hill nursery, little Dana asked her mother a big question: “What are we?” The answer still makes her smile.
stories.said: “We are Aristocrats”

stories.text: The family called Dad’s Freemason nights “the Mau Mau”. Dana took it literally and insisted to her furious teacher her father was a member.
Her first newspaper appearance: winning a rosette at the local gymkhana, legs in a sideways splits on the saddle like a Thelwell cartoon.
Great Aunt Lucy took Dana to meet Sir Edmund Hillary, but all she really remembers is shaking hands with Sherpa Tensing.
While her parents watched Prince Philip play polo, Dana watched the Maharajah and Maharani of Jaipur. It sparked her lifelong pull to India.
Her first crush was 13-year-old Laurie London on ‘6.5 Special’. Then came Elvis in ‘Love Me Tender’ at the local cinema in Woking.
Falling from a goal post, Dana fractured her skull and felt a flash of light, as if she had seen the whole Universe in a single second.
Her first public singing: a talent contest backed by The Four Camillos, judged by Tarzan star Lex Barker, Jane Fonda and Roger Vadim.
Dana was a bridesmaid five times, and never the bride, thank goodness. She never wanted to change her name for anyone.
stories.said: “I never wanted to change my name for anyone”
stories.alt: Black and white photo of two small girls in white bridesmaid dresses and bonnets, one holding flowers, petting a dachshund.

stories.text: At three, Dana went to a fancy dress party with her sister Nixi. At home they had a huge dressing up cupboard full of interesting costumes.
At Francis Holland School, music teacher Miss Muriel Ashby bent the rules and let Dana play jazz on the piano instead of classical music.
At 16 Dana cruised the Thames with the Rolling Stones for a stunt. Her job: look amazed, then drop her champagne glass. It made British Pathé News.
stories.alt: Black and white photo of teenage Dana with long fair hair, shading her eyes with her hand on a boat on the Thames.

stories.text: A yellow battery record player led to her big love: Bessie Smith’s ‘Empty Bed Blues’, played over and over in her top-floor room.
Dana took a newspaper delivery boy’s job, saved every penny, and bought a plain white Ajax drum kit at Drum City on Shaftesbury Avenue.
In thick London fog, Dana walked past Harrods with her skirt over her head, just so she could one day say she’d done it.
Strapped on a sledge after the avalanche, Dana was asked what she wanted. Irwin Shaw piled Mars Bars on her chest. Her hands were strapped in!
stories.said: “Chocolate” I replied weakly”

stories.text: British Junior Waterski champion for four years, Dana often skied in freezing water in a wetsuit that filled up and made her look like a Michelin Man!
On her way to have her appendix out, Dana took her guitar and a fluffy white seal for company. The photo later went on a 2018 album reissue.
At one of Dana’s first folk gigs, at The Tavern in East Dereham in 1965, Norfolk relatives came for moral support. The Continentals supported her!
Dana’s first paid gig: folk guitar at the opening of a new garage in Taunton. Folk in a petrol station, she admits, doesn’t really work too well.
stories.said: “Folk music in a petrol station doesn’t really work too well”

stories.text: Paul Simon lived round the corner. Dana arrived to find him packing: ‘Sound of Silence’ had become a freak Number One in America.
At sixteen Dana wrote a song for ‘The Secrets of the Windmill Girls’ and foolishly sold it outright for £25, then sang it in the film.
Paid £25 a concert in Great Yarmouth, sixteen-year-old Dana hitchhiked there and sometimes slept under the tarpaulin of a pleasure boat on the beach.
stories.said: “My mother would have had a fit had she known where I was”

stories.text: One Christmas Day, climbing a Spanish mountain near Ronda, Dana thought of her mum and cried. From then on she always spent Christmas with her.

themes.name: The blues
themes.blurb: Bessie Smith, Clapton, Dylan and seventy albums

stories.text: Yardbirds manager Giorgio Gomelsky looked after the Stones but never had them under contract. Andrew Loog Oldham stole them from under his nose.
A yellow battery record player led to her big love: Bessie Smith’s ‘Empty Bed Blues’, played over and over in her top-floor room.
At the Marquee in Wardour Street, Dana tried never to miss the Yardbirds. Eric Clapton was her favourite: he played straight from the heart.
Eric Clapton was lined up as her guitar teacher, until ‘For Your Love’ hit the charts. He wrote to postpone, in perfect Italic handwriting.
At the American Folk Blues Festival in Richmond her hero was Howlin’ Wolf, but Dana had to catch public transport home for school before he played.
Donovan played guitar on Dana’s first single, ‘Donna Donna’, in 1965. Weeks later ‘Catch the Wind’ was a hit, and Donovan was a star.
On ‘Ready Steady Goes Live’, sixteen-year-old Dana sang ‘Love is Strange’, the song Bowie had taught her, with the Les Reed orchestra.
Jimmy has come to see Dana and The London Blues Band at the 606 Club in Chelsea, and the band always buzz when they know he’s in the audience.
Dylan asked for Dana as opening act on his 1997 British tour. Two days before, he turned up at her door and they drank fennel tea.
Needing a drummer at three days’ notice for Wembley with Dylan, Dana rang Queen’s Roger Taylor. He said yes and refused the paltry fee.
stories.said: “He was an absolute angel”

stories.text: Before the tour Dylan told Dana he liked her songwriting, especially ‘Blue Temptation’, and at Wembley he listened to her whole set.
stories.said: “This was high praise indeed from His Bobness”

stories.text: John Paul Jones and Jimmy Page, later Led Zeppelin, played on Dana’s Decca sessions. Jimmy produced her single ‘You Just Gotta Know My Mind’.
With the late Mike Vernon producing and blues group Savoy Brown, Dana’s second LP was done in days. Cover: Dana on a coffin, stuffed animals all around.
Signed to Starlight Artists alongside Fleetwood Mac, Dana met Peter Green at his guitar peak, and later sang on Danny Kirwan’s solo album.
On tour in Boston, Dana sat almost at Muddy Waters’ feet at Paul’s Mall, Pinetop Perkins on piano, under a ceiling she could nearly touch.
Hobbling in on a stick with no sheet music, Dana sat at the piano and sang ‘Organ Grinder Blues’. She won the lead in West End musical ‘Mardi Gras’.
Little Feat, Joe Cocker and Bob Marley recorded upstairs at Island Studios. Word of Dana’s 16-year-old drummer Simon Phillips brought players down.
For 20 years Dana and Basil Charles ran the Mustique Blues Festival. Her festival CDs raised money for children on neighbouring St. Vincent.
stories.alt: Dana in a bright pink outfit singing on an outdoor stage beside guitarist Ian Siegal in a white suit and bandana.

stories.text: Nigel Kennedy joined the London Blues Band at the Mustique Blues Festival: not his usual style! Ronnie Wood, a friend since the sixties, played too.
Big Jay McNeely turned professional on sax in 1949, the year Dana was born. They made a duets album, Cherry Pie, and his honking sax wowed Mustique.
stories.alt: Dana and saxophonist Big Jay McNeely singing together into microphones on stage, a bass guitarist behind them.

stories.text: Hearing bottleneck Blues across a crowded Vienna café, Dana sang her way through the crowd to the guitarist: Erik Trauner of the Mojo Blues Band.
After a few songs in the cellars of Jazzland, the late owner Axel Melhardt offered Dana a gig on the spot. Decades later she still goes back to sing.
After nearly five years of court battles over Mainman, Dana had to rebuild her career. She wanted passion, not pop, and found it in the Blues.
Dana pitched Ace Records an album of the rudest old Blues she could find, called ‘Blue Job’. Boss Ted Carroll roared with laughter and signed her.
An old man’s scratchy cassette in Dubai gave Dana a melody. It became ‘Move Your Body Close To Me’, which won the Golden Carinthia and hit the charts.
At Zurich’s ‘82’ Club, Dana and the band played five 45-minute sets a night for ten days, fuelled by trips to Sprungli, the High Temple of Chocolate.
stories.said: “Yes, five!!!”

stories.text: Years before, Dana had asked Baba silently to swing in her heart whenever she sang. When she sang the Blues for Him, He rocked on His swing.
stories.said: “Please dearest Baba, will You swing whenever I sing?”

stories.text: Dana sold her beloved Citroën DS, ‘the Goddess’, to boogie-woogie pianist Joachim Palden. She visits it in Vienna, and wrote ‘Crazy ’Bout My DS’.
Dana wrote dozens of ‘Blue’ songs. Black is too moody, brown too boring, and orange doesn’t rhyme with anything, so only BLUE would do!
Dana sang over Christmas and New Year at Darjeeling’s Hotel Windemere, where the sun would burst through to reveal Kanchenchunga, Tiger Mountain.
In 1994 Dana and The London Blues Band played the Mick Ronson memorial concert at the Hammersmith Odeon, alongside Roger Daltrey and Roger Taylor.
stories.alt: Black and white photo of Mick Ronson in a straw hat beside Dana at the Château d'Hérouville

stories.text: Dana ran the Mustique Blues Festival with Basil for 20 years, and went back in 2020 for its 25th anniversary with keyboard star Dino Baptiste.
At South by Southwest in 2023, The Zombies’ Colin Blunstone reminded Dana they nearly went skinny-dipping in the Serpentine, but the car broke down.
After over 70 albums, Dana made her first of mostly covers, First Love, co-produced by Marc Almond. Gered shot the sleeve, 56 years after her first.
For Sai Baba’s 70th birthday He asked for Dana’s Western music, so she sang the Blues to a stadium crowd, with songs like ‘I Sigh For You’.
After closing time at Basil’s Bar, Dana sang the Blues unaccompanied while Basil swung along. Together they dreamed up the Mustique Blues Festival.
In 2005 Mick Jagger sang ‘Dust My Broom’ and ‘Going Down’ at the Mustique Blues Festival with Dana’s London Blues Band. The bar was packed!
Dana’s 2002 British Council tour of India covered eleven cities and twenty-two concerts, and not one bag was lost or one plane late.
When the London Blues Band played Astana’s glass pyramid, a smartly dressed Kazakh audience got so excited that ladies rushed the stage to dance.
Dana lost count long ago, so she was surprised to hear ‘Under My Bed’ was her 70th album, just as she turned 70. Feet up? Not likely.
stories.said: “I’m already plotting what to do for my next production”

stories.text: Julian Clary picked two of Dana’s songs on Desert Island Discs, and chose her Sanskrit song as the one record he’d keep above all others.
stories.said: “Thank you, Julian”

stories.text: Dana still records, still gigs and still gets a buzz from making music for other people to enjoy.
stories.said: “I won’t ever give up; I’ll continue till I’m in my wooden overcoat”
stories.alt: Dana, with red hair, sits hugging an acoustic 12-string guitar in front of shelves of blue glassware.

stories.text: Now in her eighth decade, Dana feels blessed to be still out there rolling.
stories.said: “I’m going to bop till I drop!”
stories.alt: Dana, with red hair and a pink and white floral shirt, leans on a railing beside a pool in a tropical garden.

themes.name: Sai Baba
themes.blurb: India, faith and singing for Sai Baba

stories.text: While her parents watched Prince Philip play polo, Dana watched the Maharajah and Maharani of Jaipur. It sparked her lifelong pull to India.
Falling from a goal post, Dana fractured her skull and felt a flash of light, as if she had seen the whole Universe in a single second.
Swept into the Rhine as a small child, Dana says a strange Being dressed all in white lifted her out and laid her safely on the lawn.
Seeing Sai Baba’s photo on Dana’s wall, Bob Dylan laughed. George Harrison had told him all about Him.
stories.said: “That’s the guy who materialises jewellery”

stories.text: Leaving Dana’s in 1997, Dylan said he was visiting George Harrison the next day. So Dana gave him some of her Sanskrit albums to pass on to George.
Dylan browsed Dana’s bookshelves and took a book of quotations from world religions. It inspired her own book and CD, ‘Mirrors of Love’.
From age 15 Dana had visions of nine bearded men in blue turbans. Twenty years later, in Marrakesh, the same nine walked on stage.
Dana went to Puttaparthi expecting Sai Baba to welcome her with open arms. She sat at the back, and kept coming back.
stories.said: “He never actually spoke to me for 12 years”

stories.text: Elton’s assistant Mike Hewitson played him one of Dana’s Sanskrit albums. His verdict? Dana can’t blame him: Sanskrit music isn’t to everyone’s taste.
stories.said: “Oh, I don’t like that at all”

stories.text: For Dylan’s 50th birthday in 1991 a paper asked his friends for gift ideas. Dana’s: a ticket to India, to show him a good time so he’d smile more.
Years before, Dana had asked Baba silently to swing in her heart whenever she sang. When she sang the Blues for Him, He rocked on His swing.
stories.said: “Please dearest Baba, will You swing whenever I sing?”

stories.text: From 1990 to 2015 Dana travelled to Puttaparthi every November for Sai Baba’s birthday, and sometimes sang to Him and the enormous crowds.
stories.alt: Dana in a sari stands behind Sai Baba, in a yellow robe, and singer Parween Sultana in a red sari on a decorated stage.

stories.text: A sister of the Jam Saheb of Jamnagar met Dana’s father at a London club about 50 years ago. She gave Dana her first book about Sai Baba.
Sitting at Fatehpur Sikri, Dana feels what she always feels in India.
stories.said: “I always feel in my heart that I am coming home!”

stories.text: At Sai Baba’s 75th birthday, His elephant Sai Gita joined the procession, with flags from all over the world, Vedic chanters and marching bands.
In the mid-eighties, with nothing to read on a night train from Davos, Dana borrowed ‘Man of Miracles’. By Vienna she knew she must go to India.
stories.said: “How little I knew”

stories.text: At her first sight of Sai Baba, from the back row, Dana felt deep peace and knew she must give up meat. She has not touched it since.
Crying in the Bhajan Hall, Dana silently asked Sai Baba for a sign: one beat with His left hand. He gave it without missing a beat.
stories.said: “I want You to beat time for me once with Your left hand”

stories.text: Dana smuggled her bhajan tape into darshan tucked into her clothes. Sai Baba walked straight up to her and asked for it.
stories.said: “Ah, the singer! Give me the cassette”

stories.text: Sai Baba lent Dana seven of His students as a band, and when they asked to stay nameless, He told her otherwise.
stories.said: “You must introduce each boy to the audience, by name”

stories.text: At a wedding in Cairo Dana booked a gentle dawn camel ride round the pyramids. The owner only had an over-sprightly Arab pony that wanted to gallop.
When Sai Baba asked Dana’s mother her religion, she gave her answer, and He gave her a diamond crucifix she wore until the day she died.
stories.said: “Swami, I’m Church of England, Protestant”

stories.text: Dana’s father never went to India, but he bought her first ticket there. Years later, Sai Baba told her something she always knew.
stories.said: “Your father was a very great soul”

stories.text: Sai Baba left His body on April 24th 2011, the very day Dana finished mixing ‘Mata Mata’. She still thinks of Him daily.
stories.said: “I feel no different now than when He was alive”

stories.text: For Sai Baba’s 70th birthday He asked for Dana’s Western music, so she sang the Blues to a stadium crowd, with songs like ‘I Sigh For You’.
Dana lost her voice the day before Baba’s 70th. She prayed, strangers handed her cloves and vibhuti, and about sixty per cent of her voice came back.
After singing for Sai Baba, Dana’s shoe broke and her knee ached, so she limped barefoot through the streets back to her room.
stories.said: “Treat both situations as equal”

stories.text: Dana once asked Sai Baba what life means. His answer was five words long.
stories.said: “Play the Game. Be happy!”

stories.text: In Uzbekistan a grandmother wept at Sai Baba’s photo. Then a young boy looked over her shoulder.
stories.said: “That’s the guy I was playing football with, in the street yesterday!”

stories.text: Ill for ten days in Russia, Dana was nursed by a rescued black kitten who lay purring on her neck. She named him Santosh, meaning happiness.
As Sai Baba served the savoury food, Dana silently wished for dessert. Without turning round, He stirred a bowl of paysam and handed it to her.
Before Baba’s 75th Birthday concert the sky was full of rain clouds. He waved His hand, and by the time Dana went on most of the clouds had gone.
stories.said: “Well, Swami, I’m from London where it rains a lot, so I’m used to it”

stories.text: On Dana’s 50th birthday Sai Baba showered her with rice and named her for the tiger-print cushion she always sat on (not real skin, of course).
stories.said: “Ah, Tiger!”

stories.text: Sai Baba pretended to be horrified at the words ‘Ladies Choir’ in Dana’s letter, then smiled and said yes. The choir became The Shanti Sisters.
stories.alt: A large ladies choir in turquoise saris lined up in front of an ornate, flower-decked temple building in Puttaparthi.

stories.text: On Dec. 9th 2010 Dana sang for Sai Baba for the last time. He gave her an orange glass bird, and Jorg later put it on the cover of ‘Mata Mata’.
stories.said: “It’s the Phoenix Bird, it’s the Phoenix Bird, it’s the Phoenix Bird”

stories.text: Dana ends her memoir with one of Sai Baba’s sayings, the way she wants to live.
stories.said: “Start the day with Love, Spend the day with Love”

themes.name: Funny stories
themes.blurb: Mishaps, near misses and great lines

stories.text: A milkman spotted her in cowboy boots and a Davy Crockett hat. At ten she told her mother everyone must call her Dana: she was going to be famous.
stories.said: “Here’s Dangerous Dana from Alabama”

stories.text: Tucked into the Fishers Hill nursery, little Dana asked her mother a big question: “What are we?” The answer still makes her smile.
stories.said: “We are Aristocrats”

stories.text: The family called Dad’s Freemason nights “the Mau Mau”. Dana took it literally and insisted to her furious teacher her father was a member.
Dad installed a marble fountain trickling onto Dana’s goldfish, Mrs. Perkins, just to watch dinner guests give in and dash for the loo.
As Dana’s mother clawed up the slope after the avalanche searching for her, an Englishman handed her an invitation to a ski club drinks party.
stories.said: “Ah, Mrs Gillespie, I’ve been looking for you”

stories.text: Her new band was practising on the top floor when part of the floor fell in on her sister Nixi’s bedroom. The drums went to the basement.
Dana and best friend Carrots sat down to play ‘Oranges and Lemons’ and laughed so hard not one note was played. No school choir for her!
In thick London fog, Dana walked past Harrods with her skirt over her head, just so she could one day say she’d done it.
Strapped on a sledge after the avalanche, Dana was asked what she wanted. Irwin Shaw piled Mars Bars on her chest. Her hands were strapped in!
stories.said: “Chocolate” I replied weakly”

stories.text: When Dana brought David downstairs, her father thought she’d had a girlfriend with her. David’s long lemon-yellow hair was misleading!
Covering ‘Back Home’, Elton John, David Byron and Dana had to sing as the entire 30-man England World Cup squad, and couldn’t stop giggling.
Paul Simon lived round the corner. Dana arrived to find him packing: ‘Sound of Silence’ had become a freak Number One in America.
Mid-song Tom Jones handed Dana his bolero jacket in the wings. After his act he took it back, kissed her, and fled by boat before the fans.
stories.said: “Heady stuff for a 16-year-old who was still learning the ropes”

stories.text: No ticket for the CBS party at the Dorchester? Dana followed a canapé waiter through staff corridors and emerged via a hidden mirrored door.
Bouncers charged through the crowd to throw Dana out, but Bob Dylan stepped forward to kiss her hello and the bouncers retreated.
Dana appears in ‘Don’t Look Back’, waiting in an empty Albert Hall. Manager Al Grossman reckoned she sang while surfing. It was water skiing.
stories.said: “Al Grossman says she sings while surfing”

stories.text: Dana gave Dylan her flowery bellbottoms, he wore them filming, and she was left with nothing much to wear, stuck in the hotel till he got back.
Beatles and Stones played new tracks in Dylan’s suite; John Lennon passed out on the bed Dana was sleeping in. She was in it, he was on it.
Dana’s minder John Bindon, not recognising the scruffy visitor, told Bob Dylan to get lost at her New York show. Poor Bindon later felt awful.
On cheap ‘Top of the Pops’ cover LPs Dana sang beside Reg Dwight, who told them he’d changed his name to Elton John.
stories.said: “It was one of the best moves he ever made”

stories.text: Singing five songs a night for £25 a week at the Crazy Horse Saloon, Dana ordered vodka and orange, minus the vodka, and pocketed the pound.
Visiting Israel over Christmas 1967, Dana dashed into the sparkling Red Sea at Eilat and came straight back out, face to face with an octopus.
stories.said: “I wasn’t expecting that!”

stories.text: Lost on horseback with Ashton, Gardner and Dyke, Dana headed for the nearest light. It was a funeral home, and they rode right in.
When the famous Palace Theatre stage doorman Charles retired, the Evening Standard asked his best memory of all his years there.
stories.said: “Whenever Dana Gillespie came in”

stories.text: To win a Hammer Films part, Dana fasted 21 days on water and lemon juice. She got the role, then rediscovered the crew’s food trolley.
In ‘The Lost Continent’ Dana wore two huge balloons on her shoulders. Watching incognito in Fulham, she heard the audience fall about laughing.
stories.said: “Thank goodness no one recognised me on their way out”

stories.text: Dana and David Bowie both auditioned for the stage show of ‘Hair’, on different days. Neither of them got chosen!
Dana told the whole Superstar cast David Bowie was in the audience. To her horror, David and Angie left at the interval!
stories.alt: Polaroid of David and Angie Bowie lounging

stories.text: In rock opera Catch My Soul, Othello’s dagger blade flew out over the audience. He had to slay Desdemona with just the handle!
Othello clutched his bald, made-up head in grief and left ten white fingerprints. He looked like an alien and the whole stage shook with laughter.
When P.J. Proby missed his cue in Catch My Soul, Dana was stuck alone on stage with the vital handkerchief for about five minutes. An eternity!
Dana met Colin Tennant on the Cotton House steps in a striped pyjama suit. ‘You look ready for bed,’ she said. ‘And so do you!’ he laughed.
A misprint turned Dana’s song ‘Fine and Fancy Free’ into ‘Fine and Fanny Free’. Then the promo for her ‘Big Boy’ album called it ‘Bog Boy’!
Signing to RCA, Dana told boss Rocco she loved his artist Charlie Rich. Rich’s contract had run out three weeks earlier. He then had a smash hit.
At a Macaroni Beach lunch with Dana’s house party, Princess Margaret set one guest straight on how to address her.
stories.said: “You must call me Ma’am, which rhymes with spam”

stories.text: On Mustique, Dana saw Princess Margaret mouthing the words to the saucy ‘King Size Papa’. Her secret? Her father, the King, used to sing it to her.
Dana pitched Ace Records an album of the rudest old Blues she could find, called ‘Blue Job’. Boss Ted Carroll roared with laughter and signed her.
Told Istanbul’s Pera Palas Hotel was full, Dana rang straight back with a new name. They found her a double room right away.
At the Stones’ 2006 Twickenham show, as Keith Richards stepped forward for a solo, the lady sitting behind Dana leant forward proudly.
stories.said: “That’s my son up there”

stories.text: Dana smuggled her bhajan tape into darshan tucked into her clothes. Sai Baba walked straight up to her and asked for it.
stories.said: “Ah, the singer! Give me the cassette”

stories.text: At a wedding in Cairo Dana booked a gentle dawn camel ride round the pyramids. The owner only had an over-sprightly Arab pony that wanted to gallop.
In Darjeeling at Christmas, Dana sang ‘It Ain’t Necessarily So’ to a room of nuns, then remembered the chorus line about the Bible.
Dana’s old ringtone was a sung call to prayer, but at airports people backed away from her. Now it’s something sillier.
stories.said: “I have since changed my ringtone to a quacking duck”

stories.text: Dana learned all about life from Tintin. She has a Captain Haddock rug, Tintin plates, bowls and mugs in her kitchen, and a pair of Tintin slippers.
As Sai Baba served the savoury food, Dana silently wished for dessert. Without turning round, He stirred a bowl of paysam and handed it to her.
On Dana’s 50th birthday Sai Baba showered her with rice and named her for the tiger-print cushion she always sat on (not real skin, of course).
stories.said: “Ah, Tiger!”

stories.text: Sai Baba pretended to be horrified at the words ‘Ladies Choir’ in Dana’s letter, then smiled and said yes. The choir became The Shanti Sisters.
stories.alt: A large ladies choir in turquoise saris lined up in front of an ornate, flower-decked temple building in Puttaparthi.

stories.text: These days Dana’s idea of bliss is a tapestry on her knee, a purring cat nearby and a bar of chocolate. She has made over one hundred cushions.
stories.said: “How Rock ‘n’ Roll is that!”
